source_batch.unit_label: BRBL Module A unit 5: public sector, private sector, regional rural, differentiated, co-operative and local area banks

facts.statement: State Bank of India (courseware): the State Bank of India was established under Section 3 of the State Bank of India Act, 1955 to take over the undertaking of the Imperial Bank and to carry on the business of banking and other business in accordance with the Act. It is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal and can sue and be sued in its name. The majority of shares are held by the Government of India and no shareholder other than the Government can exercise voting rights above ten per cent unless otherwise specified by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank. Its central office is the corporate centre in Mumbai; local head offices are in Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and other places decided by the Central Government in consultation with the Central Board. The Central Board has general superintendence and direction; it works on business principles with regard to public interest. The Central Government can give directions on matters of policy involving public interest in consultation with the Governor of the Reserve Bank and the Chairman of the State Bank, and the directions are given through the Central Board. The Board makes regulations to carry out the Act, in consultation with the Reserve Bank and with the prior sanction of the Central Government. Composition: a Chairman, not more than four Managing Directors appointed by the Central Government, and other directors appointed to represent workmen and officers, nominated by the Central Government from persons with special knowledge of co-operatives and rural economy, and elected by shareholders other than the Reserve Bank. The Chairman and Managing Directors hold office for a period not exceeding five years and are eligible for reappointment; the Central Government can terminate service with three months notice or pay in lieu after consulting the Reserve Bank. Local boards are set up at each place where there is a local head office (Section 21B). Business: the State Bank acts as agent of the Reserve Bank at places where it has a branch and the Reserve Bank does not, to transact Government business; apart from this it carries on banking as defined in Section 5(b) and business under Section 6(1) of the Banking Regulation Act and may acquire other banks with the sanction of the Central Government or if so directed. Accounts and audit: the books are closed and balance sheets prepared each year on 31 March; within three months the balance sheet and profit and loss account with the auditors report and a report by the Central Board on the working and activities of the State Bank are furnished to the Central Government and the Reserve Bank. The audit is by a person qualified under Section 226 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 141 of the 2013 Act); no director, member of a local board, committee or officer of the bank is eligible; the appointment is by the Reserve Bank with the previous approval of the Central Government; the auditors report and the report of the Central Board are laid before Parliament; within two months particulars of the shareholders as on that date are sent to the Government and the Reserve Bank; the annual general meeting is held within six weeks of sending the balance sheet. Subsidiary banks: there were seven subsidiary banks; State Bank of Saurashtra and State Bank of Indore were merged earlier, and on 15 February 2017 the Central Government approved the merger of five associate banks (State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur, State Bank of Hyderabad, State Bank of Travancore, State Bank of Mysore, State Bank of Patiala) and Bharatiya Mahila Bank with SBI with effect from 1 April 2017. The Central Government may make rules under Section 49 and the State Bank may make regulations with the approval of the Reserve Bank.

Regional Rural Banks (courseware): Regional Rural Banks were set up from 1975 under the Regional Rural Banks Ordinance, 1975, replaced by the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976, because the ethos and attitude of the existing banks were not fully conducive to the credit needs of rural people. The preamble describes the object as developing the rural economy by providing credit and other facilities for agriculture, trade, commerce, industry and other productive activities in rural areas, particularly for small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans and small entrepreneurs. Section 3 authorises the Central Government to establish a Regional Rural Bank by notification at the request of a sponsor bank, to operate within specified local limits; the sponsor bank holds 35 per cent of the issued capital, the Central Government holds 50 per cent and the State Government holds the remaining fifteen per cent as the courseware states. Every RRB is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal; it is generally allotted a compact area of operation of a few districts with homogeneous agro-climatic and rural conditions; it can accept all types of deposits from the public and engage in banking as in Section 5(b) of the Banking Regulation Act. Management vests in the board of directors, which works on business principles with due regard to public interest; the board makes regulations to give effect to the Act in consultation with the sponsor bank and with the previous approval of the Central Government, which can give directions on matters of policy involving public interest. The board consists of a chairman appointed by the sponsor bank from among its officers in consultation with NABARD or otherwise by the Central Government in consultation with NABARD; the chairman is whole-time and removable by the sponsor bank in consultation with NABARD and in other cases in consultation with the Central Government. A person who is adjudicated insolvent or convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude is disqualified as a director, and absence from three consecutive board meetings without leave of the board results in vacation of office. Business: an RRB may carry on Section 5(b) banking and business under Section 6(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, but the main business is granting loans and advances to small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans, small entrepreneurs, agricultural marketing societies, farmers service societies and self-help groups within the notified area. Accounts and audit: books are closed on 31 March or another date the Central Government specifies; auditors with the approval of the Central Government qualified under Section 226 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 141 of the 2013 Act); the auditors report and report on the working are laid before Parliament; the sponsor bank is empowered to monitor the progress of the RRBs by inspection, internal audit and scrutiny. Amalgamation: two or more RRBs may be amalgamated by the Central Government by notification, with provision for continuation of service of employees, binding on all parties; since 2012-13 amalgamation and consolidation were carried out to cut overheads and widen operations.

Nationalised banks (courseware): apart from SBI, the other public sector banks are called nationalised banks because they came into being through the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and 1980 (the Bank Nationalisation Acts), by which the undertakings of 20 existing private banks were transferred to the corresponding new banks. The whole paid-up capital was taken over by the Central Government; later most were listed after public issues. The 2006 Amendment (Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) and Financial Institutions Laws (Amendment) Act, 2006) lets the banks raise capital by public issue, preferential allotment or private placement of equity or preference shares, but the Central Government must hold not less than fifty-one per cent of the equity at all times, and no shareholder other than the Central Government may exercise voting rights above one per cent of total voting rights. Each nationalised bank is a body corporate with perpetual succession, can sue and be sued, and carries on banking as in Section 5(b) and other business in Section 6(1) of the Banking Regulation Act; with SBI and private banks they act as financial supermarkets through branches or subsidiaries. The board has general superintendence, direction and management of affairs and follows policies laid down by the Reserve Bank and the Central Government; the Central Government may issue directions on public interest matters in consultation with the Governor of the Reserve Bank. Section 9 of the Acts empowers the Central Government to make schemes in consultation with the Reserve Bank; the schemes (Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme, 1970 and 1980) are laid before Parliament, are binding, and deal with constitution of the board, appointment of chairman and managing director, terms of whole-time directors, disqualification and vacation of office, board meetings, committees, increase in paid-up capital and other matters. Section 19 empowers the board to frame regulations with the consent of the Reserve Bank and Central Government. Directors appointed or nominated by the Central Government: a Chairman and Managing Director (in bigger banks a separate Chairman and a Managing Director and CEO); not more than four other whole-time directors; one director who is an official of the Central Government; one director with expertise in regulation or supervision of commercial banks nominated on the recommendation of the Reserve Bank; one representing workmen employees; one representing officers; one chartered accountant with at least fifteen years of experience nominated in consultation with the Reserve Bank; and up to six other directors nominated by the Central Government. Shareholders other than the Central Government may elect up to three directors. Fit and proper criteria apply to every director and the Reserve Bank notified in 2019 stricter fit and proper directions for elected directors. Meetings (Section 12 of the Schemes): at least six times a year and at least once in each quarter; the meeting may be held by video conferencing or other electronic means; ordinarily not less than fifteen days notice; business other than that for which the meeting was convened requires the consent of the Chairman and a majority of directors present unless one weeks written notice was given to the Chairman; the quorum is one-third of the directors holding office. Committees (Sections 13 and 13A and 14): the Management Committee and the Credit Approval Committee have powers delegated by the board; other committees may be constituted to advise.

Banking Regulation Act and public sector banks (courseware): Section 51 of the Banking Regulation Act lists the sections of the Act applicable to the State Bank, nationalised banks (corresponding new banks) and Regional Rural Banks; the other sections are not applicable because the State Bank Act and the Nationalisation Acts contain provisions which modify or override them. The applicable sections (as tabulated in the courseware) include: Section 10 (prohibition of employment of managing agents and restrictions on certain forms of employment); Sections 13 to 15 (restriction on commission, brokerage and discount on sale of shares, prohibition of charge on unpaid capital, restrictions on payment of dividend); Section 17 (reserve fund); Sections 19 to 21A (restrictions on subsidiaries, RBI power to regulate advances and similar); Sections 23 to 28 (restrictions on opening and transfer of places of business, maintenance of a percentage of assets); Section 29 except sub-section 3 (accounts and balance sheet); Section 29A (associate enterprises); Section 30(1B), (1C) and (2) (special audit and auditors); Section 31 (submission of returns); Section 34 (accounting provisions not retrospective); Section 35 (inspection by the Reserve Bank); Section 35A (directions); Sections 35AA and 35AB (insolvency resolution directions and directions on stressed assets); Section 36 except 1(d); Sections 45Y to 45ZF (preservation of records, return of paid instruments, nomination for deposits, lockers and safe custody); Sections 46 to 48 (penalties, cognizance of offences, imposition of penalties); Section 50 (claims for compensation barred); Section 52 (rule-making power); Section 53 (power of the Government to exempt). Disinvestment: the State Bank of India Act was amended by the State Bank of India (Amendment) Act, 1993 so that capital is divided into shares of Rs 100 each, and the restriction on voting rights (two hundred votes) was changed to up to ten per cent. The Nationalisation Act of 1970 (and 1980) was amended in 1994 and 1995 for public holding of shares: the authorised capital could be Rs 1,500 crore divided into shares of Rs 10 each, with authority to increase or reduce between Rs 1,500 crore and Rs 3,000 crore, voting rights of shareholders limited to one per cent per shareholder, a register of shareholders, and Section 10A amended to allow dividends with earlier balance of profits to be transferred. The courseware also describes the August 2019 mega merger of 10 public sector banks into four, effective 1 April 2020, and a Government move to privatise.

Co-operative banks: applicability (courseware): co-operative banks are registered under State co-operative societies laws or under the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act; a bank operating only in one State is governed by the State law and a bank operating in more than one State is governed by the Central Act; the State or Central law governs constitution and related matters, but banking business is regulated by the Banking Regulation Act as applicable to co-operative societies, subject to modifications in Part V (Section 56), made applicable by the Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1965. Section 5(cci) defines a co-operative bank as a State co-operative bank, a central co-operative bank and a primary co-operative bank. A primary co-operative bank means a co-operative society, other than a primary agricultural credit society, which satisfies: (i) its primary object or principal business is the transaction of banking business; (ii) the paid-up share capital and reserves are not less than Rs 1 lakh; (iii) its bye-laws do not permit admission of any other co-operative society as a member except by subscribing to the share capital out of funds provided by the State Government. A State co-operative bank is the principal co-operative society in a State with the primary objective of financing other societies; a central co-operative bank is the principal society in a district with the primary objective of funding other co-operative societies in the district. A reference to a banking company in the Act is read as a reference to a co-operative bank. Name: no co-operative society other than a co-operative bank may use bank, banker or banking as part of its name, and a co-operative bank must use at least one of these words; exempt are a primary credit society, a society formed for the protection of mutual interests of co-operative banks or land development banks, and a co-operative society formed by employees of the State Bank, a subsidiary, a nationalised bank or a co-operative bank (other than a primary credit society) or of a primary credit society or land development bank. Paid-up capital and reserves: not less than Rs 1 lakh to commence or carry on banking business (Section 11 as applicable); this does not apply to a primary credit society which becomes a primary co-operative bank, for two years, extendable by one year; the real and exchangeable value of paid-up capital and reserves counts and the Reserve Bank decision on a dispute is final. Cash reserve: co-operative banks other than scheduled co-operative banks and scheduled State co-operative banks maintain in India by way of cash reserve with itself or by way of balance in a current account with the Reserve Bank or with the State or district central co-operative bank, an amount not less than three per cent of demand and time liabilities in India on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight; for scheduled primary co-operative banks and State co-operative banks the reserve is as per Section 42 of the RBI Act. Restrictions on loans (Section 20 as applicable): no loans on the security of own shares; no unsecured loans or advances to any of its directors; no unsecured loans to firms or private companies in which a director is partner, managing agent or guarantor, or to individuals where a director is guarantor; and no unsecured loans to a company in which the chairman is managing agent or chairman or managing director. The courseware notes that these restrictions do not apply to unsecured loans against bills for supplies to Government or bills of exchange arising from bona fide trade transactions; and that from 1 October 2003 the Reserve Bank prohibited co-operative banks from providing, renewing secured or unsecured loans and advances or any other funded or non-funded financial accommodation to their directors and their relatives and to firms or companies in which relatives are interested.

Co-operative banks: licensing, liquid assets, accounts, inspection and deposit insurance (courseware): a co-operative society needs a licence from the Reserve Bank under Section 22 (as applicable) to carry on banking business, but primary credit societies are exempt; societies carrying on banking at the commencement of the 1965 Act were exempt for a period of one year, had to apply for a licence within three months of commencement, and a primary credit society that becomes a primary co-operative bank applies within three months of becoming one; after applying, it can continue until its licence is rejected. Branches: prior permission of the Reserve Bank to open a new place of business or change its location except within the same city, town or village; temporary branches up to one month at an exhibition, conference or mela are allowed; opening or changing location of branches by a central co-operative bank within its area of operation is exempt; the application of a co-operative bank for permission to open a branch, other than a primary co-operative bank, is routed through NABARD with an advance copy to the Reserve Bank. Liquid assets (Section 24(1) as applicable): co-operative banks maintain liquid assets; balances with the Reserve Bank or with a State co-operative bank and central co-operative bank are counted; Section 24(2A) liquid assets not less than 25 per cent or other percentage not exceeding forty per cent as the Reserve Bank may notify, maintained at the close of business on any day; a return is filed with the Reserve Bank and, other than by a primary co-operative bank, a copy to NABARD. Accounts: the balance sheet and profit and loss account are prepared as at the last working day of the year in the forms in the Third Schedule; three copies with the statutory auditor report are submitted to the Reserve Bank within six months; a State co-operative bank and a central co-operative bank submit such return to NABARD also. Inspection: Section 35 applies with minor modifications; the Reserve Bank may call for inspection of a primary co-operative bank by officers of the State co-operative bank in the State where the primary bank is registered, and may supply a copy of the inspection or scrutiny report to the State co-operative bank or the Registrar of Co-operative Societies. Deposit insurance: the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961 applies to co-operative banks; under Section 13C co-operative banks must be registered with the corporation; the registration may be cancelled if the bank is prohibited from accepting deposits, its licence is cancelled, it is ordered wound up, it has ceased to be an eligible co-operative bank, it has converted into a non-banking co-operative society, it is amalgamated with another co-operative bank, or it has transferred its deposit liabilities. An eligible co-operative bank under Section 2(gg) is one whose law provides that an order for winding up, or sanctioning a scheme of compromise, arrangement, amalgamation or reconstruction, can be made only with the previous sanction in writing of the Reserve Bank, that a winding up order may be made if the Reserve Bank requires, and that supersession of the board and appointment of an administrator for a period not exceeding five years in aggregate is made if the Reserve Bank requires; the liquidator, insured bank or transferee must repay the Corporation under Section 21. Section 13D: the Reserve Bank may requisition winding up of a co-operative bank if it fails to comply with Section 11 capital requirements, its licence is cancelled, it is prohibited from taking fresh deposits under Section 35(4) or Section 42(3A)(b) of the RBI Act, it continues to contravene the Act after notice, it is unable to pay its debts, or a compromise cannot be worked or its continuance is prejudicial to depositors. A co-operative bank is deemed unable to pay its debts if on the returns the Reserve Bank is of opinion that it is unable to pay, or if it refused a lawful demand within two working days where the Reserve Bank has an office, branch or agency, or within five working days elsewhere, and the Reserve Bank certifies it cannot pay.

Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 (courseware): the Act was enacted on 29 September 2020 but is deemed to have come into force on 26 June 2020, except Section 4, which, in so far as it relates to primary co-operative banks, is deemed to have come into force on 29 June 2020, and in so far as it relates to State co-operative banks and central co-operative banks, comes into force on a date the Central Government notifies (with different dates possible). The Act replaced the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Ordinance, 2020 and brought 1,482 urban and 58 multi-State co-operative banks under the supervision of the Reserve Bank. Salient features: the Reserve Bank may initiate a scheme for reconstruction or amalgamation of a bank, including a co-operative bank (Section 45); once the Reserve Bank imposes a moratorium on a bank it cannot grant any loans or make investments in any credit instruments during the moratorium (amended Section 45(3)); co-operative banks may issue equity, preference or special shares on face value or at a premium to members or persons residing in their area of operations, and unsecured debentures or bonds with maturity of ten years or more, but prior approval of the Reserve Bank is required (Section 56 as applied to Section 12); no person is entitled to demand payment on surrender of shares issued to him (Section 12 as applied); the Reserve Bank may exempt a co-operative bank or a class from specified provisions mainly relating to employment, qualification of the board and appointment of a chairman, by notification (Section 53A); and the Reserve Bank may supersede the board of a multi-State co-operative bank for up to five years in the public interest and to protect depositors (new Section 36AAA).

Private sector banks (courseware): private sector banks are those in which the majority stake is held by private individuals or entities; they are mostly incorporated under the Companies Act and bound by the Banking Regulation Act and the Reserve Bank Act. There are two categories: old private sector banks that came into existence before 1968 and new private sector banks incorporated after the 1990s (the courseware counts 21 banks as at 31 March 2021). Many new banks have thrived because they were free from baggage, started with a clean slate and used advanced technology to provide error-free, quick and efficient services to a mostly affluent clientele. Most of the bigger private banks established after the 1990s were set up under the Companies Act and follow the Banking Regulation Act along with the former statute.

Differentiated banks (courseware): differentiated banks are those that cater to the needs of a specific sector or a certain demographic segment of the population; they function in a niche segment and may be defined as those that offer a limited range of services or functions under a different regulatory dispensation, or differ in capital requirement or scope of activities or area of operations. The concept was first discussed in 2007; urban co-operative banks, primary agricultural credit societies, regional rural banks and local area banks existed before 2007 and may be considered differentiated banks as they operate in localised areas. The Reserve Bank discussion paper Banking Structure in India: The Way Forward (August 2013) suggested a transition path to a differentiated bank model. The Committee headed by Shri Nachiket Mor (Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low-Income Households) proposed two designs: the Horizontally Differentiated Banking System (HDBS), in which banks specialise in one or more of payments, deposits and credit, and the Vertically Differentiated Banking System (VDBS), in which a full-service bank gives all services but is differentiated on size, geography or sector. Niche institutions exist in other countries (for example postal savings in South Korea, GE Capital for credit and payments, MasterCard and Visa for payments only). Advantages: unlocking of specialisation, long-term infrastructure lending needing high risk management expertise, very low ticket unsecured credit, filling gaps in MSME financing through asset and cash flow based lending, operating leases and factoring, customised risk management and regulatory compliance, and better price discovery and reduced intermediation cost. Payments banks: the Reserve Bank issued the key features of payments banks in November 2014 with the objectives of providing small savings accounts and payments and remittance services to migrant labour workforce, low income households, small businesses and other unorganised sector entities; eligible promoters include non-bank pre-paid payment instrument issuers, individuals or professionals, non-banking finance companies, corporate business correspondents, mobile telephone companies, supermarket chains and companies, real sector co-operatives and public sector entities; the promoter or group should be fit and proper with a sound track record of professional experience for at least five years; payment banks may accept demand deposits, issue ATM and debit cards but not credit cards, provide payment and remittance services, act as business correspondent of another bank and distribute simple non-risk sharing financial products such as mutual funds and insurance products; they cannot undertake lending activities; they invest at least 75 per cent of demand deposit balances in SLR eligible Government securities or treasury bills of maturity up to one year and hold a maximum of 25 per cent in time or fixed deposits with other scheduled commercial banks; they must maintain the cash reserve ratio; a payments bank has the minimum paid-up equity capital of Rs 100 crore and a leverage ratio of not less than 3 per cent; the promoter contribution is 40 per cent for the first five years (all figures as in the 2014 and 2016 circulars and recorded in the courseware as dated). Small finance banks: the November 2014 guidelines aimed at furthering financial inclusion by providing savings vehicles and supplying credit to small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries and unorganised sector entities through high technology and low cost operations; the bank primarily does basic banking of acceptance of deposits and lending to unserved and underserved sections; there is no restriction on area of operations; the minimum paid-up equity capital is Rs 100 crore; the promoter contribution is at least 40 per cent initially, brought down to 26 per cent within 12 years; they are subject to cash reserve and statutory liquidity requirements as for other scheduled commercial banks and must lend 75 per cent of adjusted net bank credit to priority sectors with at least 50 per cent of the loan portfolio in loans up to Rs 25 lakh. The courseware also records 2019 on-tap licensing guidelines and the August 2022 permission to act as authorised dealer category-I.

Local Area Banks (courseware): in 1996 a decision was taken to allow the establishment of Local Area Banks in the private sector to bridge gaps in credit availability and enhance the institutional credit framework in rural and semi-urban areas and provide efficient and cost-effective financial intermediation services. The minimum start-up capital was expected to be Rs 5 crore with promoters bringing the entire minimum share capital up-front; the NRI contributions to equity and the holding by a family among the promoter group should not exceed 40 per cent of the capital within three years from the date of licensing; the voting rights of an individual shareholder are restricted to ten per cent under Section 12(2) of the Banking Regulation Act. Norms: the area of operation is usually restricted to a maximum of three geographically contiguous districts; LABs finance agriculture and allied activities, small scale industries, agro-industrial activities, trading and non-farm sectors and comply with norms regarding lending to MSME, priority sector and weaker sections; they are registered as public limited companies under the Companies Act, as partnership firms under the Partnership Act, or as limited liability partnerships, are licensed under the Banking Regulation Act and may be included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act; they are subject to prudential norms, accounting policies and other policies laid down by the Reserve Bank; supervision lies with the relevant department of the Reserve Bank; at the time of grant of licence a LAB may open a branch in a single urban centre in each district and the remaining branches in rural and semi-urban centres. Their main function is to aid the development of the area, to provide all types of normal universal banking services and to mobilise rural savings. Of about 227 applications in 1996, the Reserve Bank approved only 10 licences; the courseware states that only two were in existence as at January 2022 (Coastal Local Area Bank Ltd, established 27 December 1999, head office Vijayawada, covering Krishna, Guntur and West Godavari districts; and Krishna Bhima Samruddhi Local Area Bank Ltd, established 28 February 2001, head office Mahbubnagar, covering Mahbubnagar, Raichur and Gulbarga districts). Their importance has become limited after the opening of differentiated banks such as small finance banks.

payload.title: State Bank of India
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Constitution:** a **body corporate** set up under **Section 3 of the State Bank of India Act, 1955** to take over the **Imperial Bank**; **perpetual succession**, a **common seal**, can **sue and be sued**.

**Ownership:** the **Government of India holds the majority**; **no other shareholder** may exercise **voting rights above 10 per cent** unless the Central Government specifies otherwise after consulting the Reserve Bank.

**Management:** the **Central Board** has **general superintendence and direction**, acting on **business principles** with regard to **public interest**. The **Central Government** may direct the bank on **public interest policy** after consulting the **Governor** and the **Chairman**, through the Central Board. **Regulations** are made by the Board **in consultation with the Reserve Bank** and with the **Central Government's prior sanction**.

**Board:** a **Chairman**, **up to four Managing Directors** appointed by the Government, plus directors for **workmen and officers**, directors nominated for **co-operative and rural economy** knowledge, and directors **elected by shareholders other than the Reserve Bank**. Chairman and MDs serve **up to five years** (re-appointable) and can be removed on **three months' notice or pay**. **Local boards** sit at each local head office (**Section 21B**).

**Business:** wherever it has a branch and the Reserve Bank has none, it acts as the **Reserve Bank's agent**; it may carry on **Section 5(b)** banking and **Section 6(1)** business and **acquire other banks** with Government sanction.

**Accounts and audit:** books closed on **31 March**; accounts, auditor's report and the **Central Board's report** are sent to the Reserve Bank and the Government **within three months**; auditor is **qualified under the Companies Act**, appointed by the **Reserve Bank with Government approval**; reports are **laid before Parliament**; shareholder particulars go **within two months**; **AGM within six weeks** of sending the balance sheet.

**Subsidiaries:** the **five associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank** merged with SBI from **1 April 2017**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: SBI is the only public sector bank under its own Act, with a board structure that differs from the nationalised banks.

payload.title: Regional Rural Banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Origin:** the **Regional Rural Banks Ordinance, 1975**, replaced by the **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976**, to serve **rural credit needs** of **small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans and small entrepreneurs**.

**Establishment (Section 3):** by **Central Government notification** at the request of a **sponsor bank**, for **specified local limits**. **Capital (as the courseware states):** **Central Government 50 per cent**, **sponsor bank 35 per cent**, **State Government 15 per cent**.

**Character:** a **body corporate** with perpetual succession; a **compact area** of a few districts with **similar agro-climatic and rural conditions**; accepts **all types of deposits**.

**Management:** the **board** acts on **business principles while keeping the public interest in view**; on policy matters involving public interest the **Central Government may give directions**. The **chairman** is a **whole-time** officer whom the **sponsor bank** appoints in **consultation with NABARD** (the Central Government may also appoint); the sponsor bank can **remove** the chairman. A director who is **adjudged insolvent** or **convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude** is **disqualified**; **absence from three consecutive meetings without leave** vacates office.

**Business:** **Section 5(b) banking** and **Section 6(1)** business, but mainly **loans to small and marginal farmers, labourers, artisans, small entrepreneurs, marketing and service societies and self-help groups** in the notified area.

**Accounts and audit:** closed on **31 March**; auditors approved by the **Central Government**; reports **laid before Parliament**; the **sponsor bank monitors** the RRB through **inspection, internal audit and scrutiny**.

**Amalgamation:** the **Central Government** may amalgamate two or more RRBs by notification, **preserving employees' service**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: RRBs combine local rural focus with ownership split between the Centre, a State and a sponsor bank.

payload.title: Nationalised banks: capital, board and meetings
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Source:** the **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980**; the **undertakings of 20 banks** passed to **corresponding new banks**. Each is a **body corporate** with **perpetual succession** that does **Section 5(b)** banking and **Section 6(1)** business.

**Capital:** under the **2006 Amendment** banks may raise **equity or preference capital** by **public issue, preferential allotment or private placement**, but the **Central Government must hold at least 51 per cent** at all times, and **no other shareholder** may exercise **voting rights above 1 per cent**.

**Control:** the **board** has **superintendence, direction and management**, following **Reserve Bank and Government policies**; the **Central Government** can give **public interest directions** after consulting the **Governor**. **Section 9** lets the Government make **schemes** (**Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Schemes, 1970 and 1980**) on the **board, chairman and MD, directors' terms, disqualification, meetings, committees and capital**; **Section 19** lets the board make **regulations** with Reserve Bank and Government consent.

**Board composition:** **Chairman and Managing Director** (a separate **Chairman** and **MD and CEO** in larger banks); **up to four other whole-time directors** (raised from three in August 2019); **one Central Government official**; **one regulation or supervision expert** on the **Reserve Bank's recommendation**; **one workmen** and **one officer** director; **one chartered accountant of at least 15 years' experience**; and **up to six other** Government nominees. **Other shareholders** elect **up to three directors**. All must be **fit and proper**.

**Meetings:** **at least six a year and at least one in each quarter**; **15 days' notice**; **quorum one-third** of directors in office; video conferencing allowed.

**Committees:** the **Management Committee** and **Credit Approval Committee** (**Sections 13 and 13A**) and other committees (**Section 14**).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 51 per cent and 1 per cent rules keep control with the Government while allowing public shareholding.

payload.title: Banking Regulation Act sections that apply to public sector banks; disinvestment and mergers
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Section 51** lists which provisions of the **Banking Regulation Act** apply to **SBI, nationalised banks and RRBs**. The rest do **not** apply because their **own statutes** modify or override them. Applicable sections include:

| Sections | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| **10** | Restrictions on employment |
| **13-15** | Commission and brokerage on shares, unpaid capital, **dividend** |
| **17** | **Reserve fund** |

payload.title: Co-operative banks: applicability, definitions and loan restrictions
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Which law:** a bank in **one State** follows the **State Co-operative Societies Act**; a bank in **several States** follows the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act**. These govern **constitution**; **banking business** is regulated by the **Banking Regulation Act** as modified by **Part V (Section 56)**, applied by the **1965 Act**.

**Definitions (Section 5(cci)):** a **co-operative bank** is a **State co-operative bank**, a **central co-operative bank** or a **primary co-operative bank**. A **primary co-operative bank** is a society **other than a primary agricultural credit society** that: (i) has **banking as its primary object or principal business**; (ii) has **paid-up share capital and reserves of not less than Rs 1 lakh**; (iii) has **bye-laws that do not admit another co-operative society as a member** (except by subscribing from State Government funds). A **State co-operative bank** is the **principal society in a State** that finances other societies, and a **central co-operative bank** is the **principal society in a district**.

**Name:** only co-operative banks may use **bank, banker or banking** (a co-operative bank must use at least one); **exempt** are **primary credit societies**, societies formed to protect the **common interest of co-operative banks or land development banks**, and certain **employees' societies**.

**Capital:** **at least Rs 1 lakh** of paid-up capital and reserves; a **primary credit society becoming a primary co-operative bank** gets **two years** (extendable by **one**); **real and exchangeable value** counts; the **Reserve Bank decides** disputes.

**Cash reserve:** other than scheduled banks, **3 per cent** of demand and time liabilities; **scheduled** banks follow **Section 42 of the RBI Act**.

**Section 20 restrictions:** **no loans on own shares**; **no unsecured loans to directors**, to **firms or private companies in which a director is partner, managing agent or guarantor**, to **individuals whom a director guarantees**, or to a **company in which the chairman is managing agent or director**. **Exceptions:** unsecured advances against **bills for supplies to Government** and **bona fide trade bills**. From **1 October 2003** the Reserve Bank **bars all credit to directors and their relatives and related firms**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The primary co-operative bank definition screens out agricultural credit societies and ties the label to a banking business.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Banking is its primary object, paid-up capital and reserves are at least Rs 1 lakh, and its bye-laws do not allow another co-operative society as a member (except through State funds).

payload.title: Co-operative banks: licensing, branches, liquid assets, accounts, inspection and deposit insurance
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Licence (Section 22):** needed to carry on banking, but **primary credit societies are exempt**. Societies already banking at the 1965 commencement had **one year** and had to **apply within three months**; a **primary credit society that becomes a primary co-operative bank** applies **within three months**; it may continue **until rejection**.

**Branches:** **prior Reserve Bank permission** to open or relocate except **within the same city, town or village**; **temporary branches** (up to **one month**) at exhibitions are free; **central co-operative banks** may open **within their area of operation**; applications go **through NABARD** with an **advance copy to the Reserve Bank** (primary co-operative banks excluded).

**Liquid assets (Section 24):** **not less than 25 per cent** (the Reserve Bank may fix **up to 40 per cent**), held on **any day**; balances with the **State or central co-operative bank** count; a **return** goes to the Reserve Bank (and **NABARD** for banks other than primary).

**Accounts:** balance sheet and profit and loss account **as on the last working day of the year**, in **Third Schedule forms**, **three copies with the auditor's report within six months** to the Reserve Bank (and **NABARD** for State and central co-operative banks).

**Inspection (Section 35):** applies with **minor modifications**; **officers of the State co-operative bank** may inspect a **primary co-operative bank**; reports may go to the **State bank or the Registrar**.

**Deposit insurance:** under **Section 13C** the bank **must be registered with the DICGC**; registration may be **cancelled** if the bank is **barred from deposits**, loses its **licence**, is **wound up**, stops being **eligible**, **converts to a non-banking society**, is **amalgamated** or **transfers its deposits**. An **eligible co-operative bank** (**Section 2(gg)**) is one whose law requires **Reserve Bank sanction for winding up, compromise, amalgamation or reconstruction** and allows **supersession of the board by an administrator for up to five years in aggregate** at the Reserve Bank's requirement.

**Winding up (Section 13D):** the Reserve Bank may **require winding up** where the bank **fails Section 11**, **loses its licence**, is **barred from deposits**, **keeps contravening** the Act after notice, is **unable to pay debts**, or a **compromise cannot be worked**. It is **deemed unable to pay** if it refuses a **lawful demand** within **two working days** (office, branch or agency of the Reserve Bank at that place) or **five working days** (elsewhere) and the Reserve Bank **certifies**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank, NABARD and the Registrar all have a role, which is why the sector faces dual control.

payload.title: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 and co-operative banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Dates:** enacted on **29 September 2020**, deemed in force from **26 June 2020**; Section 4 for **primary co-operative banks** from **29 June 2020**; for **State and central co-operative banks** from a date the Central Government notifies. It replaced the **June 2020 Ordinance** and brought **1,482 urban and 58 multi-State co-operative banks** under **closer Reserve Bank supervision**.

**Main features:**

- The Reserve Bank can start a **scheme of reconstruction or amalgamation** (**Section 45**) including for a co-operative bank.
- During a **moratorium** the bank **cannot grant loans or make investments** (**Section 45(3)**).
- Co-operative banks may issue **equity, preference or special shares** (face value or premium) to **members or residents of their area**, and **unsecured debentures or bonds of 10 years or more**, with **prior Reserve Bank approval** (**Section 12 as applied by Section 56**).
- **No right to demand payment** on **surrender** of shares.
- The Reserve Bank may **exempt** co-operative banks from provisions on **employment, qualification of directors and chairman** (**Section 53A**).
- The Reserve Bank may **supersede the board of a multi-State co-operative bank for up to five years** (**Section 36AAA**).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 2020 changes give the Reserve Bank the same corrective tools for co-operative banks as it has for commercial banks.

payload.title: Private sector banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Private sector banks** are those whose **majority stake is held by private individuals or entities**; mostly **companies under the Companies Act**, governed also by the **Banking Regulation Act** and the **Reserve Bank of India Act**.

**Two groups:** **old private sector banks** (existing **before 1968**) and **new private sector banks** (set up **after the 1990s**). The courseware counts **21** in all as at **31 March 2021** (not taught as current).

The new banks grew because they began with a **clean slate**, used **advanced technology** and served a mostly **affluent clientele** with **error-free, quick and efficient service**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Private banks follow company law as well as banking law, which is why they differ from statutory-corporation banks.

payload.title: Differentiated banks: payments banks, small finance banks, HDBS and VDBS
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Differentiated banks** work in a **niche** with a **limited range of services**, a **different regulatory dispensation**, or a different **capital requirement, scope or area**. Examples include **urban co-operative banks**, **primary agricultural credit societies**, **regional rural banks**, **local area banks**, **payments banks** and **small finance banks**.

**Nachiket Mor Committee models:**

- **HDBS (Horizontally Differentiated Banking System):** banks **specialise in one or more of payments, deposits and credit**.
- **VDBS (Vertically Differentiated Banking System):** a **full-service bank** differentiated by **size, geography or sector**.

**Advantages:** **specialisation**, **long-term infrastructure lending** by banks with the right risk skills, **small unsecured credit**, closing **MSME financing gaps** (asset and cash-flow lending, leasing, factoring), **customised regulation** and **lower intermediation cost**.

**Payments banks:** serve **migrant workers, low income households, small businesses**; accept **demand deposits**, issue **ATM and debit cards (not credit cards)**, offer **payments and remittances**, act as **business correspondent**, and **distribute simple non-risk sharing products** (mutual funds, insurance); they **cannot lend**; they **invest most deposits in short government securities** and hold the **CRR**. The courseware figures (**Rs 100 crore capital**, **3 per cent leverage**, **40 per cent promoter contribution**) are dated and not taught.

**Small finance banks:** **basic banking** (deposits and loans) to **unserved and underserved** groups: **small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries**; **no area restriction**; **CRR and SLR** as for other scheduled banks; **priority sector lending of 75 per cent of adjusted net bank credit**, with **half of the loans small** (up to **Rs 25 lakh**) (courseware, dated). The numbers are held back.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Differentiated banks widen access by letting specialists operate under tailored rules instead of full universal-bank rules.

payload.title: Local Area Banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose (1996 decision):** to **bridge gaps in credit** and provide **cost-effective financial intermediation in rural and semi-urban areas**.

**Norms (courseware):** minimum start-up capital **Rs 5 crore**, brought up-front by the promoters; **NRI** contribution and **family** holding **not above 40 per cent** within three years of licensing; **individual voting rights limited to 10 per cent** (**Section 12(2)**); **area of operation usually up to three geographically contiguous districts**; **registered as a public limited company**, a **partnership firm** or an **LLP**; **licensed under the Banking Regulation Act** and may be on the **Second Schedule**; subject to **Reserve Bank prudential norms**; **priority sector and MSME lending norms** apply. A LAB may open **one branch in an urban centre** in each district at the start, the rest in **rural and semi-urban centres**.

**Role:** to **mobilise rural savings** and invest them **locally** and provide **normal universal banking services**.

**Present position (courseware):** of about **227 applications**, **10 licences** were approved; **two** LABs were operating as at **January 2022**. Their relevance has **declined** with **small finance banks**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: LABs were meant to tie local deposits to local credit, but few survived.

items.title: State Bank of India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Constitution:** a **body corporate** set up under **Section 3 of the State Bank of India Act, 1955** to take over the **Imperial Bank**; **perpetual succession**, a **common seal**, can **sue and be sued**.

**Ownership:** the **Government of India holds the majority**; **no other shareholder** may exercise **voting rights above 10 per cent** unless the Central Government specifies otherwise after consulting the Reserve Bank.

**Management:** the **Central Board** has **general superintendence and direction**, acting on **business principles** with regard to **public interest**. The **Central Government** may direct the bank on **public interest policy** after consulting the **Governor** and the **Chairman**, through the Central Board. **Regulations** are made by the Board **in consultation with the Reserve Bank** and with the **Central Government's prior sanction**.

**Board:** a **Chairman**, **up to four Managing Directors** appointed by the Government, plus directors for **workmen and officers**, directors nominated for **co-operative and rural economy** knowledge, and directors **elected by shareholders other than the Reserve Bank**. Chairman and MDs serve **up to five years** (re-appointable) and can be removed on **three months' notice or pay**. **Local boards** sit at each local head office (**Section 21B**).

**Business:** wherever it has a branch and the Reserve Bank has none, it acts as the **Reserve Bank's agent**; it may carry on **Section 5(b)** banking and **Section 6(1)** business and **acquire other banks** with Government sanction.

**Accounts and audit:** books closed on **31 March**; accounts, auditor's report and the **Central Board's report** are sent to the Reserve Bank and the Government **within three months**; auditor is **qualified under the Companies Act**, appointed by the **Reserve Bank with Government approval**; reports are **laid before Parliament**; shareholder particulars go **within two months**; **AGM within six weeks** of sending the balance sheet.

**Subsidiaries:** the **five associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank** merged with SBI from **1 April 2017**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: SBI is the only public sector bank under its own Act, with a board structure that differs from the nationalised banks.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 3 of the State Bank of India Act, 1955.

items.title: Regional Rural Banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Origin:** the **Regional Rural Banks Ordinance, 1975**, replaced by the **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976**, to serve **rural credit needs** of **small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans and small entrepreneurs**.

**Establishment (Section 3):** by **Central Government notification** at the request of a **sponsor bank**, for **specified local limits**. **Capital (as the courseware states):** **Central Government 50 per cent**, **sponsor bank 35 per cent**, **State Government 15 per cent**.

**Character:** a **body corporate** with perpetual succession; a **compact area** of a few districts with **similar agro-climatic and rural conditions**; accepts **all types of deposits**.

**Management:** the **board** acts on **business principles while keeping the public interest in view**; on policy matters involving public interest the **Central Government may give directions**. The **chairman** is a **whole-time** officer whom the **sponsor bank** appoints in **consultation with NABARD** (the Central Government may also appoint); the sponsor bank can **remove** the chairman. A director who is **adjudged insolvent** or **convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude** is **disqualified**; **absence from three consecutive meetings without leave** vacates office.

**Business:** **Section 5(b) banking** and **Section 6(1)** business, but mainly **loans to small and marginal farmers, labourers, artisans, small entrepreneurs, marketing and service societies and self-help groups** in the notified area.

**Accounts and audit:** closed on **31 March**; auditors approved by the **Central Government**; reports **laid before Parliament**; the **sponsor bank monitors** the RRB through **inspection, internal audit and scrutiny**.

**Amalgamation:** the **Central Government** may amalgamate two or more RRBs by notification, **preserving employees' service**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: RRBs combine local rural focus with ownership split between the Centre, a State and a sponsor bank.

items.title: Nationalised banks: capital, board and meetings
items.core_explanation_md:
**Source:** the **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980**; the **undertakings of 20 banks** passed to **corresponding new banks**. Each is a **body corporate** with **perpetual succession** that does **Section 5(b)** banking and **Section 6(1)** business.

**Capital:** under the **2006 Amendment** banks may raise **equity or preference capital** by **public issue, preferential allotment or private placement**, but the **Central Government must hold at least 51 per cent** at all times, and **no other shareholder** may exercise **voting rights above 1 per cent**.

**Control:** the **board** has **superintendence, direction and management**, following **Reserve Bank and Government policies**; the **Central Government** can give **public interest directions** after consulting the **Governor**. **Section 9** lets the Government make **schemes** (**Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Schemes, 1970 and 1980**) on the **board, chairman and MD, directors' terms, disqualification, meetings, committees and capital**; **Section 19** lets the board make **regulations** with Reserve Bank and Government consent.

**Board composition:** **Chairman and Managing Director** (a separate **Chairman** and **MD and CEO** in larger banks); **up to four other whole-time directors** (raised from three in August 2019); **one Central Government official**; **one regulation or supervision expert** on the **Reserve Bank's recommendation**; **one workmen** and **one officer** director; **one chartered accountant of at least 15 years' experience**; and **up to six other** Government nominees. **Other shareholders** elect **up to three directors**. All must be **fit and proper**.

**Meetings:** **at least six a year and at least one in each quarter**; **15 days' notice**; **quorum one-third** of directors in office; video conferencing allowed.

**Committees:** the **Management Committee** and **Credit Approval Committee** (**Sections 13 and 13A**) and other committees (**Section 14**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 51 per cent and 1 per cent rules keep control with the Government while allowing public shareholding.

items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 51** lists which provisions of the **Banking Regulation Act** apply to **SBI, nationalised banks and RRBs**. The rest do **not** apply because their **own statutes** modify or override them. Applicable sections include:

| Sections | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| **10** | Restrictions on employment |
| **13-15** | Commission and brokerage on shares, unpaid capital, **dividend** |
| **17** | **Reserve fund** |
| **19-21A** | **Subsidiaries**, **Reserve Bank power over advances** |
| **23-28** | **Places of business**, **percentage of assets** |
| **29** (except 3), **29A** | **Accounts** and **associate enterprises** |
| **30(1B), (1C), (2)** | **Special audit** and **auditors** |
| **31** | **Returns** |
| **34** | **Accounting provisions** not retrospective |
| **35, 35A, 35AA, 35AB** | **Inspection**, **directions**, **insolvency resolution and stressed assets** |
| **36** (except 1(d)) | **Reserve Bank powers** |
| **45Y-45ZF** | **Records**, **paid instruments**, **nomination**, **lockers** |
| **46-48** | **Penalties** and **cognisance** |
| **50, 52, 53** | **No compensation claims**, **rules**, **exemptions** |

**Disinvestment:** the **1993 SBI Amendment** made shares **Rs 100 each** and moved the voting cap to **up to 10 per cent**; the **1994 and 1995 amendments** to the **nationalisation Acts** allowed **public shareholding**, a **Rs 1,500 crore** authorised capital (**Rs 10 shares**, adjustable up to **Rs 3,000 crore**), a **1 per cent voting cap** and a **register of shareholders**.

**Mergers:** the courseware records the **August 2019 plan** merging 10 public sector banks into four from **1 April 2020**, with customers treated as customers of the **transferee banks**; the current count and later changes are not taught here.

items.title: Co-operative banks: applicability, definitions and loan restrictions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Which law:** a bank in **one State** follows the **State Co-operative Societies Act**; a bank in **several States** follows the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act**. These govern **constitution**; **banking business** is regulated by the **Banking Regulation Act** as modified by **Part V (Section 56)**, applied by the **1965 Act**.

**Definitions (Section 5(cci)):** a **co-operative bank** is a **State co-operative bank**, a **central co-operative bank** or a **primary co-operative bank**. A **primary co-operative bank** is a society **other than a primary agricultural credit society** that: (i) has **banking as its primary object or principal business**; (ii) has **paid-up share capital and reserves of not less than Rs 1 lakh**; (iii) has **bye-laws that do not admit another co-operative society as a member** (except by subscribing from State Government funds). A **State co-operative bank** is the **principal society in a State** that finances other societies, and a **central co-operative bank** is the **principal society in a district**.

**Name:** only co-operative banks may use **bank, banker or banking** (a co-operative bank must use at least one); **exempt** are **primary credit societies**, societies formed to protect the **common interest of co-operative banks or land development banks**, and certain **employees' societies**.

**Capital:** **at least Rs 1 lakh** of paid-up capital and reserves; a **primary credit society becoming a primary co-operative bank** gets **two years** (extendable by **one**); **real and exchangeable value** counts; the **Reserve Bank decides** disputes.

**Cash reserve:** other than scheduled banks, **3 per cent** of demand and time liabilities; **scheduled** banks follow **Section 42 of the RBI Act**.

**Section 20 restrictions:** **no loans on own shares**; **no unsecured loans to directors**, to **firms or private companies in which a director is partner, managing agent or guarantor**, to **individuals whom a director guarantees**, or to a **company in which the chairman is managing agent or director**. **Exceptions:** unsecured advances against **bills for supplies to Government** and **bona fide trade bills**. From **1 October 2003** the Reserve Bank **bars all credit to directors and their relatives and related firms**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The primary co-operative bank definition screens out agricultural credit societies and ties the label to a banking business.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Banking is its primary object, paid-up capital and reserves are at least Rs 1 lakh, and its bye-laws do not allow another co-operative society as a member (except through State funds).

items.title: Co-operative banks: licensing, branches, liquid assets, accounts, inspection and deposit insurance
items.core_explanation_md:
**Licence (Section 22):** needed to carry on banking, but **primary credit societies are exempt**. Societies already banking at the 1965 commencement had **one year** and had to **apply within three months**; a **primary credit society that becomes a primary co-operative bank** applies **within three months**; it may continue **until rejection**.

**Branches:** **prior Reserve Bank permission** to open or relocate except **within the same city, town or village**; **temporary branches** (up to **one month**) at exhibitions are free; **central co-operative banks** may open **within their area of operation**; applications go **through NABARD** with an **advance copy to the Reserve Bank** (primary co-operative banks excluded).

**Liquid assets (Section 24):** **not less than 25 per cent** (the Reserve Bank may fix **up to 40 per cent**), held on **any day**; balances with the **State or central co-operative bank** count; a **return** goes to the Reserve Bank (and **NABARD** for banks other than primary).

**Accounts:** balance sheet and profit and loss account **as on the last working day of the year**, in **Third Schedule forms**, **three copies with the auditor's report within six months** to the Reserve Bank (and **NABARD** for State and central co-operative banks).

**Inspection (Section 35):** applies with **minor modifications**; **officers of the State co-operative bank** may inspect a **primary co-operative bank**; reports may go to the **State bank or the Registrar**.

**Deposit insurance:** under **Section 13C** the bank **must be registered with the DICGC**; registration may be **cancelled** if the bank is **barred from deposits**, loses its **licence**, is **wound up**, stops being **eligible**, **converts to a non-banking society**, is **amalgamated** or **transfers its deposits**. An **eligible co-operative bank** (**Section 2(gg)**) is one whose law requires **Reserve Bank sanction for winding up, compromise, amalgamation or reconstruction** and allows **supersession of the board by an administrator for up to five years in aggregate** at the Reserve Bank's requirement.

**Winding up (Section 13D):** the Reserve Bank may **require winding up** where the bank **fails Section 11**, **loses its licence**, is **barred from deposits**, **keeps contravening** the Act after notice, is **unable to pay debts**, or a **compromise cannot be worked**. It is **deemed unable to pay** if it refuses a **lawful demand** within **two working days** (office, branch or agency of the Reserve Bank at that place) or **five working days** (elsewhere) and the Reserve Bank **certifies**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank, NABARD and the Registrar all have a role, which is why the sector faces dual control.

items.title: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 and co-operative banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Dates:** enacted on **29 September 2020**, deemed in force from **26 June 2020**; Section 4 for **primary co-operative banks** from **29 June 2020**; for **State and central co-operative banks** from a date the Central Government notifies. It replaced the **June 2020 Ordinance** and brought **1,482 urban and 58 multi-State co-operative banks** under **closer Reserve Bank supervision**.

**Main features:**

- The Reserve Bank can start a **scheme of reconstruction or amalgamation** (**Section 45**) including for a co-operative bank.
- During a **moratorium** the bank **cannot grant loans or make investments** (**Section 45(3)**).
- Co-operative banks may issue **equity, preference or special shares** (face value or premium) to **members or residents of their area**, and **unsecured debentures or bonds of 10 years or more**, with **prior Reserve Bank approval** (**Section 12 as applied by Section 56**).
- **No right to demand payment** on **surrender** of shares.
- The Reserve Bank may **exempt** co-operative banks from provisions on **employment, qualification of directors and chairman** (**Section 53A**).
- The Reserve Bank may **supersede the board of a multi-State co-operative bank for up to five years** (**Section 36AAA**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 2020 changes give the Reserve Bank the same corrective tools for co-operative banks as it has for commercial banks.

items.title: Private sector banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Private sector banks** are those whose **majority stake is held by private individuals or entities**; mostly **companies under the Companies Act**, governed also by the **Banking Regulation Act** and the **Reserve Bank of India Act**.

**Two groups:** **old private sector banks** (existing **before 1968**) and **new private sector banks** (set up **after the 1990s**). The courseware counts **21** in all as at **31 March 2021** (not taught as current).

items.title: Differentiated banks: payments banks, small finance banks, HDBS and VDBS
items.core_explanation_md:
**Differentiated banks** work in a **niche** with a **limited range of services**, a **different regulatory dispensation**, or a different **capital requirement, scope or area**. Examples include **urban co-operative banks**, **primary agricultural credit societies**, **regional rural banks**, **local area banks**, **payments banks** and **small finance banks**.

**Nachiket Mor Committee models:**

- **HDBS (Horizontally Differentiated Banking System):** banks **specialise in one or more of payments, deposits and credit**.
- **VDBS (Vertically Differentiated Banking System):** a **full-service bank** differentiated by **size, geography or sector**.

**Advantages:** **specialisation**, **long-term infrastructure lending** by banks with the right risk skills, **small unsecured credit**, closing **MSME financing gaps** (asset and cash-flow lending, leasing, factoring), **customised regulation** and **lower intermediation cost**.

**Payments banks:** serve **migrant workers, low income households, small businesses**; accept **demand deposits**, issue **ATM and debit cards (not credit cards)**, offer **payments and remittances**, act as **business correspondent**, and **distribute simple non-risk sharing products** (mutual funds, insurance); they **cannot lend**; they **invest most deposits in short government securities** and hold the **CRR**. The courseware figures (**Rs 100 crore capital**, **3 per cent leverage**, **40 per cent promoter contribution**) are dated and not taught.

**Small finance banks:** **basic banking** (deposits and loans) to **unserved and underserved** groups: **small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries**; **no area restriction**; **CRR and SLR** as for other scheduled banks; **priority sector lending of 75 per cent of adjusted net bank credit**, with **half of the loans small** (up to **Rs 25 lakh**) (courseware, dated). The numbers are held back.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Differentiated banks widen access by letting specialists operate under tailored rules instead of full universal-bank rules.

items.title: Local Area Banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose (1996 decision):** to **bridge gaps in credit** and provide **cost-effective financial intermediation in rural and semi-urban areas**.

**Norms (courseware):** minimum start-up capital **Rs 5 crore**, brought up-front by the promoters; **NRI** contribution and **family** holding **not above 40 per cent** within three years of licensing; **individual voting rights limited to 10 per cent** (**Section 12(2)**); **area of operation usually up to three geographically contiguous districts**; **registered as a public limited company**, a **partnership firm** or an **LLP**; **licensed under the Banking Regulation Act** and may be on the **Second Schedule**; subject to **Reserve Bank prudential norms**; **priority sector and MSME lending norms** apply. A LAB may open **one branch in an urban centre** in each district at the start, the rest in **rural and semi-urban centres**.

**Role:** to **mobilise rural savings** and invest them **locally** and provide **normal universal banking services**.

**Present position (courseware):** of about **227 applications**, **10 licences** were approved; **two** LABs were operating as at **January 2022**. Their relevance has **declined** with **small finance banks**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: LABs were meant to tie local deposits to local credit, but few survived.
